**@e-learningenglish** (👍11 · 2024-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=53SIKuCuHv0&lc=UgyIOgCehA1GGeukVFl4AaABAg
  Great video, Adam!  I’d like to add 5 more that can be very helpful for all language learners:  
  1.	Write down new words: It's a really good idea to write down useful new vocabulary.
  2.	 Read in English: Reading graded books, articles, or short stories in English helps you see how words are used in sentences.
  3.	Watch videos: Watching videos in English can help you hear how words are pronounced and used in everyday conversation.
  4.	Learn from Context: When you come across a new word, make sure to look up its meaning and try to use it in a sentence.
  5.	Use It or Lose It!
  Practice using new words in your speaking and writing. The more you use a word, the more likely you are to remember it. 
  "Remember, practice, practice, practice makes masters."

**@fragmented_fragrance** (👍100 · 2021-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=53SIKuCuHv0&lc=UgyOwdRilm0ktfuw6wN4AaABAg
  Among what you've recommended in this video are these four tips that I find most useful and works for many including myself.
  1. Read and listen to as much as you can; There's no need for further explanation to this all-time top priority. You can search and use so many materials on the Internet that comes in handy without having to paying even one single penny for them just like this channel. Yet in order not to be lost in an avalanche of information, I suggest sticking with only one material at a time until you get a full understanding of it instead of searching ridiculously for more and more. Trust me on that. Biting off more than you can chew most likely ends up being another form of procrastination.
  2. Use an English-English dictionary; This will increasingly help stop you from translating English into your mother tongue whenever you bump into those 'recognizable yet not clear' words, one major contributor to slowing down your comprehension and thought process while reading. Make sure to get into a habit of looking up new words in an English-English dictionary, otherwise you will never be able to catch a wealth of subtleties each word carries. And the next time you meet those words in context, try to reconstruct their meaning in your own way based on what you can remember from the English definitions.
  3. Learn as many synonyms as you can; This has very much to do with the previous one in that they all facilitate the process of retrieving the meaning and usage of words in a much faster way. When I happen to see newly learnt words or phrases while reading(which is a real bonus), I automatically think of other words that can be used interchangeably or make up my own expressions on the spot in order to make them more firmly ingrained in my memory. In this way, I've seen a certain degree of improvement in my writing skills as well.
  4. Write at least 150 words every day without the help of a dictionary; Even when you've taken all three steps previously mentioned, chances are that you still find yourself not knowing how to properly use those new words in your own writing. Learning a language is indeed a painful experience since the moment you think you completely made sense of it, it turns its back on you right away. But don't panic! It's no more than a sign that you haven't got the most out of those words yet. While making it a point to include those 'getting on your nerves' words in your writing, make as many mistakes as possible and be a little more forgiving to yourself. Of course, it won't happen overnight but have a belief in yourself that you can pull it off at the end of the day!

  Thanks Wes! 
  
  1. ubiquitous ~ existing or being everywhere
  2. cumbersome ~ difficult or burdensome
  3. facetious ~ not meant to be taken seriously
  4. arduous ~ requires strenuous effort; difficult
  5. presumptuous ~ showing lack of respect by doing something that you shouldn't
  6. pensive ~ deep or serious thought
  7. circuitous ~ not straight or direct (circuitous route, path)
  8. conscientious ~ morally responsible for doing work carefully and treating others with respect
  9. meticulous ~ showing great attention to detail
  10. convoluted ~ difficult to follow; complex; twisted (convoluted sentence, argument, story)
  11. germane ~ relevant; closely or significantly related 
  12. preposterous ~ contrary to reason; ridiculous; absurd 
  13. perfunctory ~ performed merely as a routine; habit; duty
  14. truculent ~ fierce; cruel; aggressively hostile 
  15. austere ~ severe in manner; strict; without excess
  16. capricious ~ subject to sudden or unpredictable change
  17. defamatory ~ false or unjustified harm to someone’s reputation 
  18. esoteric ~ understood by a select few who have special knowledge 
  19. nascent ~ beginning to exist or develop 
  20. quintessential ~ representing the most perfect or typical example

      42. reluctantly ~ in an unwilling and hesitant way. ( "he reluctantly agrees to do his duty" )
      43. unabashedly  ~ taking a stand on what we did or said without any fear or hesitation ( "he was staring unabashedly at her")
      44. vaguely  ~ in a way that is unclear or uncertain ( i vaguely remember my childhood memories )
      45. fervently  ~ excitement  to do something ( she woke  and prayed fervently for an answer )
      46. diligently ~  work hard and carefully ( she spent her time diligently on fiver to get a client )
      47. vicariously ~experienced through the activities of other people, rather than by doing something yourself ( The reader of adventure stories wants romance and excitement vicariously.
      48. hastily ~ to perform any task very fast  because we have a very short period of time ( i punched him hastily in the last round of sparring ) 
      49. utterly ~  totally, completely ( your shirt is utterly  fantastic )
      50. intently ~ completely focused, doing something  with full of attention (He was watching her intently again)

      31. quid pro quo ~  means “this for that”  something in exchange for something. it can be a favor or  anything ( you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours)

      37. malaise ~ a vague feeling of uneasiness as a sign of the early stage of illness ( have you ever experienced the  malaise or vague  feeling ?)
      38.  Sycophant ~ a person who praises someone to get some advantage ( there were  many sycophants around the boss)
      39.  dilettante ~ you can use dilettante to talk about someone, who seems interested in a subject, but does not know very much about that,( she thing she is an expert in food and sciences but trust me she is a dilettante )
      40. zenith ~ a top or a peak of something ( in 1992 khan  was at the zenith of his achievements )

    ↳ **@NickyLobuky** (👍5 · 2025-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uLN6IdRtDhg&lc=UgyxnamJb0sCij9m5D54AaABAg.9akYVD1mEIiA7ILf_EcHei
      Here are some vocabulary and useful expressions for working as a hostess in a restaurant:
      
      Greeting Customers
      
      1. "Welcome to [Restaurant Name]!"
      2. "Hi, how many are in your party?"
      3. "Right this way, please."
      4. "I'll be happy to seat you."
      
      Managing Waitlists
      
      1. "It'll be about a [X] minute wait."
      2. "I can put you on the waitlist, or you can wait at the bar."
      3. "We'll call your name when your table is ready."
      4. "I apologize for the wait, we're running a bit behind."
      
      Seating Customers
      
      1. "Follow me, please."
      2. "Here's your table, enjoy your meal!"
      3. "Can I start you off with some water or bread?"
      4. "Your server will be with you shortly."
      
      Handling Special Requests
      
      1. "I can accommodate that, let me check on availability."
      2. "We have a table by the window available."
      3. "I can seat you in a quieter area if you'd like."
      4. "We're happy to accommodate special occasions, let me see what I can do."
      
      Communicating with Staff
      
      1. "Table for [X] ready."
      2. "We need a high chair/booster seat."
      3. "Can we get some extra utensils/napkins?"
      4. "I need to move this table to a different section."
      
      Farewell
      
      1. "Thanks for dining with us, come back soon!"
      2. "Have a great day/evening!"
      3. "We appreciate your business."
      4. "See you next time!"
      
      Some additional expressions:
      
      - "We're fully booked" (no availability)
      - "I can offer you a reservation at [time]" (alternative option)
      - "We have a waitlist available" (option to wait)
      - "I'll be happy to call you when your table is ready" (offering to call)
      
      Remember to be friendly, organized, and attentive to customers' needs!

    ↳ **@NickyLobuky** (👍3 · 2025-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uLN6IdRtDhg&lc=UgyxnamJb0sCij9m5D54AaABAg.9akYVD1mEIiA7ILtPV93My
      Here are some vocabulary and useful expressions for working as a hostess in a restaurant:
      
      Greeting Customers
      
      1. "Welcome to [Restaurant Name]!"
      2. "Hi, how many are in your party?"
      3. "Right this way, please."
      4. "I'll be happy to seat you."
      
      Managing Waitlists
      
      1. "It'll be about a [X] minute wait."
      2. "I can put you on the waitlist, or you can wait at the bar."
      3. "We'll call your name when your table is ready."
      4. "I apologize for the wait, we're running a bit behind."
      
      Seating Customers
      
      1. "Follow me, please."
      2. "Here's your table, enjoy your meal!"
      3. "Can I start you off with some water or bread?"
      4. "Your server will be with you shortly."
      
      Handling Special Requests
      
      1. "I can accommodate that, let me check on availability."
      2. "We have a table by the window available."
      3. "I can seat you in a quieter area if you'd like."
      4. "We're happy to accommodate special occasions, let me see what I can do."
      
      Communicating with Staff
      
      1. "Table for [X] ready."
      2. "We need a high chair/booster seat."
      3. "Can we get some extra utensils/napkins?"
      4. "I need to move this table to a different section."
      
      Farewell
      
      1. "Thanks for dining with us, come back soon!"
      2. "Have a great day/evening!"
      3. "We appreciate your business."
      4. "See you next time!"
      
      Some additional expressions:
      
      - "We're fully booked" (no availability)
      - "I can offer you a reservation at [time]" (alternative option)
      - "We have a waitlist available" (option to wait)
      - "I'll be happy to call you when your table is ready" (offering to call)
      
      Remember to be friendly, organized, and attentive to customers' needs!

      Here are some vocabulary and phrases related to shopping in a mall:
      
      General Shopping
      
      1. Store directory
      2. Mall map
      3. Sales associate
      4. Fitting room
      5. Cashier
      6. Payment method (cash, credit card, etc.)
      7. Shopping bag
      8. Receipt
      
      Asking for Help
      
      1. "Where can I find...?"
      2. "Do you have...?"
      3. "What's the price of this?"
      4. "Can I try this on?"
      5. "Do you have this in a different size/color?"
      
      Making a Purchase
      
      1. "I'll take this, please."
      2. "Can I pay with...?"
      3. "Do you accept...?"
      4. "Can I get a refund/exchange?"
      5. "Can you gift wrap this?"
      
      Comparing Prices
      
      1. "How much is this?"
      2. "Is this on sale?"
      3. "Do you have a discount coupon?"
      4. "Can I price match?"
      5. "What's the difference between these two?"
      
      Other Useful Phrases
      
      1. "I'm just browsing."
      2. "Can you hold this for me?"
      3. "Do you have a loyalty program?"
      4. "Can I get a shopping cart/basket?"
      5. "Where is the food court/restroom?"
      
      Some additional vocabulary:
      
      - Aisle
      - Clearance
      - Discount
      - Promotion
      - Return policy
      - Shopping cart/basket
      - Store hours
      
      Remember to practice your English skills while shopping, and don't hesitate to ask for help if you need it!

      One’s vocabulary is almost entirely dependent on the upbringing of the individual, and a result of one’s subsequent erudition. Speaking with such a vocabulary may perhaps make others feel Ill at ease because they do not understand the words being spoken to them; however, this embarrassment is rather a reflection of that person’s shortcomings and not a detriment to the speaker. I am not responsible for your feelings, or any lack of effort to understand the English language or that of any other tongue. However, speaking in this manner would suggest a rather cold and impersonal tone which creates distance between the speaker and the audience. This is why governments around the world maintain such wording. This attitude can commonly be identified as the “royal we” — and is further colloquialized by the expression “we are not amused.” 🤣

**@theforestguardianinthemoon8550** (👍30 · 2022-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uLN6IdRtDhg&lc=Ugwv3L6sFSIwAnUM08V4AaABAg
  Nouns: 
  
  1. quid pro quo - something given/taken in exchange for something else
  2. catch-22 - a problem that cannot be solved because the solution to the problem is inherent in the problem itself
  E.g.: "It's a catch-22"
  3. epitome -  something typical that represents a group as a whole
  4. dichotomy between (two things) - the contrast between two things that are opposed
  E.g.: We're studying the dichotomy between economic development and environmental protection
  5. myriad - a great number of people or things (= various)
  6. credence - the belief as to the truth of something
  E.g.: The email they discovered gave credence to his unethical behavior
  7. malaise - a vague feeling of physical discomfort or uneasiness as an early sign of an illness
  8.  sycophant -  a person who tries to gain attention by flattering wealthy or influential people
  9.  dilettante - a person who cultivates an interest in something without learning in-depth information
  10. zenith - the top; peak; highest point of something

**@Anna-mc3ll** (👍26 · 2022-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uLN6IdRtDhg&lc=Ugy4hV0ELnG_Z-cBFXB4AaABAg
  Verbs:
  
  1. to admonish - to advise against something; to scold;
  
  E.g.: “The parents admonished their child for telling a lie.”
  
  2. to advocate for something - to show strong support for something;
  
  3. to bemoan - to express distress, grief, or regret;
  
  4. to compel - to drive someone to a course of action;
  
  5. to embezzle - to take money (or property) fraudulently; to steal
  
  6. to extol - to praise highly; to laud; to eulogize;
  
  7. to impugn - to claim that something is false; to challenge something as false; to cast doubt upon (a certain situation or person);
  
  E.g.: “They tried to impugn her character with false accusations.”
  
  9. to obfuscate - to confuse something; to bewilder something; to make something unclear;
  
  10. to placate - to appease something, especially by (making) concessions;
  
  11. to repudiate - to reject something or someone with disapproval.
  
  E.g.: “The professor repudiated the students’ request to postpone the exam.”
  
  Thank you, Wes!

      I had just written a 300 word explanation as to why I disagree but it appears my phone did not want me to send that reply and promptly reloaded my web browser. This is my view on the matter: I believe that the degree of difference between British and American speakers is not enough to be considered a difference of language, it’s two different dialects of the same language **at most**. Small differences in terms and spelling is nothing majour, we see more changes in generational gaps’ slangs than we do that. If one were to consider the “dialects” incorporated by the umbrella language known as “Chinese” that only refers to Mandarin, they would realise that Britain and America have almost no differences whatsoever in how they choose to communicate. The “dialects” of “Chinese” vary so vastly that one can speak one and completely not comprehend another. There is not only pronunciation differences, but even basic structure of the different dialects can be entirely different. I.e. learning a new one is essentially the same as learning Japanese and then Latin; there is little to no correlation. If such deviation is still considered dialects of the same language, then the level of disparity between British and American English is nowhere near the degree of disparaging comments from both sides. All these do is draw a line of dialect portrayed as an astronomical divider, kept stemming from a conflict that ended centuries ago.
      
            Also, as an undergoer of American education, I would like to note that schools do teach us the proper grammar and (our) spelling*, it’s the children that are the cause for their decline, not the institution. I have had many peers that, around the fourth or fifth grade (years 5-6) are around the average for that age, but end up declining significantly within a few years’ time, mixing up apostrophes and spellings as if they’ve suddenly traveled 5 years into the past. I have also seen some who learned at an average pace and simply continue at that rate, just learning at the average rates. It is because of this that I say it is unfair to blame the schooling when it’s likely that there are many occurrences of this in learners of either type of English.
      
      *I generally prefer British spelling, but that’s simply personal preference + I use common terms interchangeably e.g. “rubbish” and “trash”

  ​There are 4 extra "m"s (commments, commment, commmment) -> 4 Minutes

  We know Hecker's spam comment (hpls1mmin2spls4hpls3spls6hmin4mpls3) is a math equation.

  ​Minutes (m): -2 + 3 = +1
  ​Seconds (s): +4 + 6 = +10
  ​This gives us an added time of + 0:01:10

      Not to umm actually all over the place, but he didn't really use chimera correctly. It doesn't really mean an impossible goal. The difference is subtle, and I know im just being pedantic, but It's more like an impossible thing you wish for and believe in rather than an unrealistic goal you're working towards and it's certainly not your vision of that unrealistic goal.
      
      Basically, her vision of a utopian society isn't a chimera.
      The concept of a utopian society by itself, however, could be.
      
      Example:
      "The utopian society envisioned by the philosopher was rejected by her critics as a chimera."
      Or
      "The philosopher envisioned a utopian society, which was rejected by her peers as a chimera."
      The way it's worded in the video would state that her vision itself is mythical, which it isn't. Unrealistic, maybe, but still real.

    ↳ **@erianle123547** (👍3 · 2025-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a1hrqxFm1Ss&lc=UgwC89zWal4dmvFW14R4AaABAg.ACnz4vyvs8gAE5ZNANU9OJ
      @  I did a quick google search that led to bit of a rabbit hole, from what I can find I think they all share the same Latin root word 'cōgere,' meaning "to drive or bring together, force, or compel." 
      
      Coalition comes from the medieval Latin word 'coalitio' meaning fusion, which itself comes from the verb 'coalescere' which is the root word for coalesce. These words first start to appear around 1500-1700.
      
      Coagulation itself comes from an even older Latin word coagulatus, which is the past participle of coagulare. Coagulare comes directly from the Latin word cogere, which means "to drive together." With Coagulation first appearing sometime between 1150—1500. 
      
      Interestingly, 'cōgere' comes from an even older verb 'cogo' meaning 'I force' in Latin, which is the root for nearly every word that starts with "con" that I can find, such as confer, control, congregation, condense, constrain, and even more words such as compel, collect, coarse, and curdle. 
      
      (This is where I went down an etymology rabbit hole, so feel free to stop here, lol.)
      
      Now, even more interesting is the origin of "cogo" itself. Firstly, Cōgō is a third conjugation verb that means "I compel" or "I gather". The root word for 'cōgō' is 'coagō' which is made up of the prefix co- and the word agō, which means "to lead, drive, impel, push".
      
      Now, this might seem fairly boring, but the reason I think this is so interesting, and one of the reasons I find entomology so fascinating, is that 'coagō' has two root words, 'agere' which is Latin for "to do" or "to drive" and ironically, 'cogo'. I say ironically because cogo's root word is coago, which itself is derivative of an older use of cogo.
      
      Cogo, is a cognate (meaning it derives from the same origin) with the root word 'cóo' found in both the Eastern Maninkakan language and Hamer-Banna language, which are now known as the Maninka and Hamer languages respectively. Hamer is native to Ethiopia, while Maninka is native to Guinea, Mali, Liberia, Senegal, Sierra Leone, and the Ivory Coast. I find this fascinating because we tend to assume Latin is the "origin" of all our words and root words, but Latin isn't actually that old of a language compared to a number of others. Cogo and cóo both share origins but it's hard to pinpoint exactly where, however it's likely that cóo is the older of the two and influenced early Latin via trade routes between speakers of the Indo-European languages and the Mande languages of West Africa.

  Innovation → is broad and general. It can mean any new idea, method, or improvement (not only tech).
  
  Example: Innovation in education has made learning more interactive.
  
  Technology / technological innovation → is specific to technology (software, machines, digital tools, AI, etc.).
  
  Example: Technological innovations such as smartphones have completely changed communication.
  
  👉 So, you cannot always replace technology with innovation.

**@Vivereftw** (👍44 · 2022-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fj88r-v7EPo&lc=UgyOK2Nz7c1bdWPSYFd4AaABAg
  Hello, native speaker here. To intensify "gorgeous," you can say "drop dead gorgeous." Also, in a lot of these phrases, "very" sounds sort of weird to English speakers, but instead of substituting for an entirely different word, we will often just replace the word "very" with a word like "really" or "super." 
  
  For instance:
  "I was super tired last night." 
  "I was really tired last night."
  
  Of course, we will also use other words like in this video. I'd say, among all the alternative words presented in the video, we would use these the most in place of a phrase like "really ____" or "super _____". (This is, of course, in my subjective experience. Other native speakers may say otherwise) :
  
  -gorgeous
  -exhausted
  -amazed
  -tiny
  -huge
  -awful
  -for "very difficult," we'd probably be most likely to just say "really hard" when referring to something that is difficult but we are perhaps already capable of doing, but we might say "challenging" if it is something that requires a lot of thought or self-improvement to overcome the obstacles
  -for "very simple," we would maybe just say that, but might also say "really basic" if simple refers to something that isn't complex, or "really easy" if it refers to something that is not difficult
  -starving
  -mad
  
  For anything not listed, it is because I think you could use the "very _____," "really _____," or "super _____" version as well as any of the alternate versions and sound like a native speaker. Again, this is just my opinion.

      I was really tired. It was really good. It was really expensive.

      I was so tired. It was so good. It was so expensive.

    ↳ **@Eapfoundation [channel author]** (👍1 · 2023-08-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cq4J8bPBcck&lc=UgzxVladz6yZ5vgwMKZ4AaABAg.9gA2aviyiwQ9hEnm8csbo0
      Hi Walidoss. That's a good question. Academic writing still contains opinions, which is why there is academic debate on any topic. Let's take a straightforward topic like climate change. Most people would agree that this is happening, but not everyone agrees, and even those who agree still disagree on the extent, the consequences, and the best way to tackle the problem. You could write a paper presenting renewable energy as the best way to tackle climate change, and that would be an opinion. But, the reader would still expect you to write objectively in terms of presenting arguments and evidence to support your opinion that renewable energy is the best solution. What other solutions are there, and why is this one better? How will it tackle the problem? What do other authors and experts say? Conclusions are often opinions, and may be 'hedged' to make them softer e.g. 'It would seem that solar energy is unlikely to be adopted on a wide scale unless the cost is drastically reduced.' Will solar energy be adopted on a wide scale? Well, it's possible, but the writer doesn't think so (and has presumably shown why, with objective evidence, earlier in the paragraph). Hope that helps.

      That's true to some extent, but we need to consider the context of the writing. For coursework at university, the writer would be expected to research in order to find out information about the topic and include it in their writing, with suitable references. For other kinds of writing, such as IELTS or TOEFL or other placement tests, the topics are usually general in nature, allowing the writer to draw on their existing knowledge, with emphasis placed on how the ideas are used and connected rather than the quality of those ideas. Sometimes topics are challenging and it is difficult for the writer to come up with ideas, but on the whole, whatever the context, the writer should be able to generate ideas and write. Would you agree with this? What is your specific context for writing?

**@Emaakha** (👍22 · 2026-05-11) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2eVSK_8j7w&lc=Ugz4kD1BAsfA1entjmF4AaABAg
  IELTS & Professional Synonyms (0:26 - 21:19):
  
  Demonstrate (0:48): Used instead of "show" when providing proof or displaying information in a professional/academic context.
  Predominantly (1:42): Use instead of "mostly" to describe something that exists in the largest part of a case.
  Enhance (2:19): A more polished way to say "improve," particularly for designs or quality.
  Consider (2:41): Use instead of "think about" when reflecting on options thoughtfully.
  State (3:14): A formal version of "say," commonly used in writing.
  Discuss (3:40): A professional alternative to "talk about."
  Reside (4:22): Use instead of "live" in legal or formal contexts.
  Modify (4:51): A precise way to say "change," suggesting a small, controlled adjustment.
  Minimize (5:27): Use instead of "reduce" to imply lowering something (like risk) as much as possible.
  Cease (6:32): A formal way to say "stop," often used in commands or legal writing.
  Attempt (6:55): Use instead of "try" to imply a serious, dedicated effort.
  Recover (7:35): A medical or formal term for "getting better" from an illness.
  Deteriorate (8:07): The professional opposite of recovering; use when health or conditions decline.
  Contemplate (8:32): A deeper, more serious version of "thinking carefully" about something.
  Refine (8:56): Use when you want to "make something better" in terms of precision or efficiency.
  Eliminate (9:32): A strong way to say "get rid of" something permanently.
  Verify (10:13): More specific than "check"; used when confirming the accuracy of information.
  Deplete (10:44): A specific term for "using up" all of a resource.
  Detrimental (13:54): A highly professional alternative to "bad," used for things that cause harm.
  Effortless (14:30): Use instead of "easy" to describe something that feels natural.
  Elevate (16:41): A metaphorical way to say "raise" a discussion or level.
  Decline (17:09): Use instead of "fall" for trends in reports.
  Prominent (17:26): A sophisticated word for "famous" or well-known.
  Boost (17:46): An energetic alternative to "increase."
  Require (18:07): Use instead of "need" for formal obligations.
  Inquire (18:31): A professional version of "ask."
  Conclude (19:19): Use instead of "end" for meetings or speeches.
  Retain (20:10): A professional way to say "keep" or "hold onto" something.
  Frequently (20:38): An advanced adverb for "a lot."
  Extended (21:03): Use instead of "a long time" to describe duration.
  Overused Words & Alternatives (21:19 - 53:00):
  
  Delightful / Pleasant (23:53): Better adjectives to replace "good" when describing experiences.
  Astute / Ingenious (28:51): Advanced alternatives to "smart" or "clever."
  Fascinating / Intriguing / Captivating (29:40): Use these to replace the overused word "interesting."
  Petrified (36:03): Use this to describe being extremely "scared."
  Courageous / Bold (36:34): Sophisticated alternatives to "brave."
  Rapid / Speedy / Brisk (37:14): Use these instead of "fast."
  Words/Phrases to Avoid (53:00 - 1:43:54):
  
  Try: It sounds weak/uncommitted. Use "will" or "commit to" instead.
  Advices: Grammatically incorrect. Use "advice" (uncountable) or "piece of advice."
  Wrong: Sounds harsh. Use "incorrect" or "not correct."
  Gonna: Informal slang. Use "going to" or formal structures for professional settings.
  Persons: Use only in legal documents; use "people" for all normal conversations.
  Ought: Outdated. Use "should."
  Works: Do not use for assignments/tasks; use "work."
  Query: Unnatural if used as a synonym for "question"; stick to "question" for general inquiries.
  Participate: Must be followed by "in." Avoid using it as a synonym for "attend."
  Funny: Use "fun" for enjoyable experiences and "funny" only for things that cause laughter.
  I will do it: Too long for a simple acceptance. Use the more natural "Will do."

  Yes, note-taking is always important. Easy answer - Cite your sources and reference them, always. It does not matter whether you are paraphrasing OR quoting a source directly.  Keep in mind that all AI is incapable of providing (thus far), accurate sources.  Using AI to 'paraphrase' is tantamount to letting the tool 'comprehend' material that any writer should attempt FIRST and summary FIRST. THEN, consider giving AI your material for improvement.   Describing things:
      Instead of very interesting    
          That book was extremely interesting
          That book was incredibly interesting
          That book was tremendously useful
          That book was particularly useful
       
          That film was dead good
          That film was extremely good
          
     Intensified adjective 
          That film was [amazing, terrific, splendid, awesome, outstanding]
   
  
  
  Describing people:
      My boss: she's a perfectly nice woman
      Yeah i think my new boss is a thoroughly nice man
      We've just moved into a new flat and the new neighbor is exceptionally friendly
      I think my new neighbor is a genuinely friendly person
      My teacher i think he's highly intelligent
      I think my english teacher is remarkably intelligent
      
  Describing activities:
      I went to a party last week and to be honest it was mind-numbingly boring
      I went to a party with my friend but it was just downright boring
      The meeting with my boss was just painfully slow
      The meetings with mr smith they are frustratingly slow
      Lady gaga's last concert was extremely bad
      The concert was really bad 
  
      Using an adjective that intensifies bad.  
      the party or the meeting was appalling
      It was an awful meeting
      What a dreadful concert 
      That was a terrible party
      That was an agonizing meeting

  Speaking test question I got on 29 April 2021 at Bangkok
  
  Part 1 (Interview)
  
  – What is your full name?
  – Can I see your ID?
  – What type of accommodation do you live in?
  – What does your accommodation look like?
  – What can you see from your windows?
  – Do you like to take breaks while working or studying?
  – What do you do on your breaks?
  – What do people in general do on their breaks?
  – Why do people take breaks?
  
  Part 2 (Cue Card)
  
  Talk about a perfect job for you. You should say
  
  – What kind of job is it?
  – How do you know about it?
  – What skills or training are required for this job?
  – And explain why you think this is a perfect job for you.
  
  Part 3 (Discussion)
  
  – In your country, what professions do young kids want to be in?
  – How do their preferences change with time?
  – What do people do to get their dream jobs?
  – Do you think working from home is advantageous?
  – Are people taking advantage of the ‘work from home’ option?
  – Is working from home a better option than working from the office?
  – Is having people work from the office better for the company?
